items.claim: The alternative recorded as rejected for this span's ending is markedly weaker than the live question the span's own discussion already raises about that same closing verse.
items.evidence: This span's own discussion leaves open, undecided, whether the first-person plea inside the closing verse (Lam.1.9) already marks the first turn to the personified city's own voice, or is only a momentary breach inside an otherwise third-person report -- the harder question this ending actually poses. The alternative recorded as rejected is a one-verse-earlier close at Lam.1.8, which would strand the refrain from the report it completes; that is an easy call, not a live contest. The stronger real rival -- that Lam.1.9's plea, rather than the fuller turn at Lam.1.12, is the true onset of personified speech -- is named in the span's own discussion but never appears as the alternative actually weighed against the chosen ending.

items.claim: The third-person voice held through both verses, the refrain-following front seam, and the forward-argued turn to personified speech at Lam.1.12 all hold up against the text.
items.evidence: Both verses keep third-person report grammar until each one's own closing plea; the alternative that Lam.1.10-Lam.1.11 already opens personified speech is correctly set aside because pronouns and verbs stay third-person up to the interjection itself. The covered letters and the parashah marks on both verses match the underlying inventories exactly, and the open question of exactly where the voice turns is honestly left unresolved rather than forced.

items.claim: The closing verse of this span is credited to the personified city's own first-person voice, but it is grammatically third-person throughout, undermining the seam warrant built on the same voice closing there.
items.evidence: Verses Lam.1.12-Lam.1.16 carry first-person forms addressed to a passing onlooker, including the first-person marker אֲנִ֣י at Lam.1.16. Lam.1.17 switches grammatical person entirely: Zion is named and described in the third person with third-person suffixes -- בְּיָדֶ֗יהָ ('her hands') and לָ֔הּ ('to her') -- and Jacob and Jerusalem are likewise described in the third person in the same verse, with no first-person form anywhere in it. This span's own account describes the personified voice as continuing through this verse before the refrain closes it, but the bytes show a third-person narrating voice at the closing verse itself, not a continuation of the personified city's own speech. No deviation is disclosed for this closing verse's person-shift, unlike the disclosed treatment given to the first-person plea embedded in Lam.1.9, which explicitly flags its own departure from a plain third-person reading.
tier_citations: byte tier: oshb:Lam.1.17 tokens בְּיָדֶ֗יהָ, לָ֔הּ

items.claim: The opening line frames the personified voice as continuing across the prior verse's refrain, but that verse is grammatically third-person, so the framing overstates continuity even though this span's own content and ending remain sound.
items.evidence: This span's content (Lam.1.18-Lam.1.22) is genuinely first-person throughout and its close at Lam.1.22 rests on the poem's own strongest available seam. But the opening line describes the personified voice as continuing past the refrain at Lam.1.17 into this span, when Lam.1.17 itself carries no first-person form -- it names Zion, Jacob and Jerusalem in the third person only. The framing borrows a continuity that the immediately preceding verse's bytes do not support; this does not change the span's own boundary or content, which stand on independent grounds, but the transition claim itself should not stand uncorrected.
tier_citations: byte tier: oshb:Lam.1.17 (no first-person form present); web:Lam.1.18 quoted verbatim

items.claim: The span defends against an interior split on the ground that a topic shift alone is not a seam, but then closes at Lam.2.9 without offering any voice- or address-based ground for stopping there rather than continuing into the equally third-person verse that follows.
items.evidence: The rejected interior split at Lam.2.6 is set aside because no voice or addressee change marks that line, only a shift in topic -- a sound standard. But the span's own ending at Lam.2.9 is defended by no comparable ground: Lam.2.10 continues the same third-person grammar with no first-person or vocative marker at the seam itself (the first first-person form in this stretch, at 'my eyes,' does not appear until Lam.2.11). By the standard the span itself invokes, a topic change alone -- from the destruction of institutions to the community's mourning response -- does not carry a seam; no voice or addressee shift is disclosed at Lam.2.9/Lam.2.10 to justify treating that line differently from the rejected Lam.2.6 split.

items.claim: The unit type applied to this span names its closing turn to direct address, but three of its four verses carry no address at all, and no deviation is disclosed for classifying the whole span by its final verse's content.
items.evidence: Lam.2.10 describes the elders and virgins in the third person; Lam.2.11-Lam.2.12 shift to the narrator's own first-person grief and the children's collapse, again without any addressee; only Lam.2.13 reaches a vocative naming its addressee. Classifying the full four-verse span as address-centered is a real, arguable choice given where the span is heading, but it labels a majority third-person/first-person-narrator stretch by its final verse alone, and no one-sentence disclosure marks this as a deviation from a plainer reading -- unlike the disclosed treatment given to the first-person plea embedded in Lam.1.9, which explicitly flags its own departure from a plain third-person reading.

items.claim: This span is described as returning to third-person report once the address to the daughter of Jerusalem ends, but the second-person address forms naming that same addressee continue unbroken through the span's own final verse.
items.evidence: The address opened two verses earlier (Lam.2.13) uses a second-person feminine suffix, as in אֲעִידֵ֞ךְ ('I testify to you'). Those same second-person forms continue through every verse of this span: נְבִיאַ֗יִךְ ('your prophets,' Lam.2.14), א֣וֹיְבַ֔יִךְ ('your enemies,' Lam.2.16), and צָרָֽיִךְ ('your adversaries,' closing Lam.2.17) all carry the addressee's own second-person form, alongside third-person narration of Yahweh's action and the enemies' quoted taunt. The addressee named at Lam.2.13 is not dropped at Lam.2.14; it persists to the end of this span. Describing the span as a plain return to third-person report, and classifying it under a third-person city unit type, does not match the second-person forms carried in its own verses.
